labs.title: Hash it yourself — integrity in your hands
labs.objective: Compute SHA-256 digests of strings and files, observe the avalanche effect, and verify a file against a published hash.
steps: This lab reworks the General Security Concepts scenario 'The download that did not match' into commands you run yourself — same concept, hands-on instead of multiple choice.
Open the Terminal tab for this bootcamp — every command below runs there.
Type exactly: echo -n "hello" | sha256sum — the output shows the well-known digest for that input
Type exactly: echo -n "hallo" | sha256sum — one letter changed, a completely different digest: the avalanche effect
Type exactly: sha256sum /etc/hosts — the digest of a real file, followed by its path
In your own words, say why a mismatched digest means you must not trust the file.

checks.hint: In the Terminal tab, run `echo -n "hello" | sha256sum`. If the check fails, confirm you typed it exactly — including the -n flag and the quotes.
In the Terminal tab, run `sha256sum /etc/hosts`. The output should end with the filename.

labs.success_message: Lab complete — you computed real SHA-256 digests and saw the avalanche effect. That is integrity verification, hands-on.

labs.title: Read the auth log like an analyst
labs.objective: Surface failed SSH login attempts from /var/log/auth.log and distinguish normal noise from a brute-force pattern.
steps: This lab reworks the Security Operations scenario 'The log file that confessed' into commands you run yourself.
Open the Terminal tab for this bootcamp — every command below runs there.
Type exactly: grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log | head -20 — the first twenty failed login lines
Type exactly: grep -c "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log — the total count of failed attempts
Type exactly: grep "Accepted" /var/log/auth.log | tail -5 — the most recent successful logins, for contrast
Decide in your own words: does the volume and pattern look like users mistyping, or an attack?

checks.hint: In the Terminal tab, run `grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log`. The matching lines themselves contain that phrase.
In the Terminal tab, run `grep "Accepted" /var/log/auth.log`. Successful logins contain the word Accepted.

labs.success_message: Lab complete — you read authentication logs the way a SOC analyst triages them: failures first, successes for contrast.

labs.title: Inspect a certificate before you trust it
labs.objective: Use openssl to read a certificate's subject, issuer, and validity dates — the same fields behind every browser padlock.
steps: This lab reworks the General Security Concepts scenario 'The browser's red warning' into commands you run yourself.
Open the Terminal tab for this bootcamp — a sample certificate server.crt is waiting in the lab directory.
Type exactly: openssl x509 -in server.crt -noout -subject -issuer — who the cert is for and who signed it
Type exactly: openssl x509 -in server.crt -noout -dates — the notBefore and notAfter validity window
Decide in your own words: is this certificate currently valid, and how would you know it expired?

checks.hint: In the Terminal tab, run `openssl x509 -in server.crt -noout -subject -issuer`. The output names the issuer.
In the Terminal tab, run `openssl x509 -in server.crt -noout -dates`. The output includes the notAfter expiry date.

labs.success_message: Lab complete — you read a certificate like an engineer: subject, issuer, validity window. Expiry will never surprise you again.

labs.title: Spot the listening services
labs.objective: List listening TCP sockets with ss and judge which services should — and should not — be exposed.
steps: This lab builds the attack-surface habit behind the Threats domain: every open port is a door; know your doors.
Open the Terminal tab for this bootcamp — every command below runs there.
Type exactly: ss -tlnp — TCP sockets in listening state, numeric, with process names
For each LISTEN line, ask: do I recognize this service, and should it face the network?
Type exactly: ss -tlnp | grep ":22" — confirm whether SSH is listening, and consider whether it should be reachable from everywhere
Write down one service you would restrict or disable, and why.

checks.hint: In the Terminal tab, run `ss -tlnp`. Listening sockets show the LISTEN state.

labs.success_message: Lab complete — you enumerated the attack surface from the inside. Fewer open doors, fewer break-ins.

labs.title: Audit the password aging policy
labs.objective: Read /etc/login.defs to find the system's password aging rules and judge whether they match policy.
steps: This lab connects the Governance domain to a real config file: policy says one thing, the system says another — find the gap.
Open the Terminal tab for this bootcamp — every command below runs there.
Type exactly: grep -E "^PASS_MAX_DAYS|^PASS_MIN_DAYS|^PASS_WARN_AGE" /etc/login.defs — the password aging directives
Compare the values against a sample policy: maximum 90 days, minimum 1 day, warn 7 days before expiry
Decide in your own words: does the system enforce the policy, or is there a finding to report?

checks.hint: In the Terminal tab, run `grep -E "^PASS_MAX_DAYS|^PASS_MIN_DAYS|^PASS_WARN_AGE" /etc/login.defs`. The matching lines name the directives.

labs.success_message: Lab complete — you audited a live config against a written policy. That gap-hunting reflex is governance in action.

labs.title: Network Recon with Nmap
labs.objective: Perform a safe, authorized service-version scan of a lab target and identify exposed services for vulnerability triage.
steps: Confirm you have written permission to scan the target — scanning without authorization is itself an attack. Use your lab VM's address (e.g., 192.0.2.10).
Run a ping sweep to confirm the target is up: nmap -sn 192.0.2.10
Run a service-version scan across all ports, showing only open ones, and save the output: nmap -sV -p- --open 192.0.2.10 -oN scan.txt
Attempt OS detection to inform your triage: nmap -O 192.0.2.10
Extract the open services and versions from your saved output: grep -E "^[0-9]+/tcp.*open" scan.txt
For the most exposed service found, note its exact version — you will check it against CVE/NVD next.

checks.hint: Start with a ping sweep: nmap -sn <target>
Run the service-version scan with -sV and --open
Add OS detection with the -O flag

labs.title: Integrity by Hash: SHA-256 in Practice
labs.objective: Use SHA-256 hashing to prove file integrity and detect tampering — the integrity leg of the CIA triad, hands-on.
steps: Create a test file: echo 'patient dose: 5mg' > dose.txt
Record its baseline hash: sha256sum dose.txt | tee baseline.txt
Verify the file against the baseline: sha256sum -c baseline.txt (expect OK)
Simulate tampering: echo 'patient dose: 50mg' > dose.txt
Re-verify: sha256sum -c baseline.txt — observe the FAILED result and compare the new digest
Reflect: which CIA leg did the hash protect, and what does this imply for software downloads and forensic images?

checks.hint: Hash the file first: sha256sum dose.txt
Verify against the baseline: sha256sum -c baseline.txt

labs.title: Log Hunting: Brute Force in auth.log
labs.objective: Hunt a brute-force login attack in Linux authentication logs using grep/awk pipelines — the analyst's daily craft.
steps: Simulate an attack from a second lab host (or a partner): generate 25 failed SSH logins against this box.
Count failed passwords per source IP: grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head
List every IP with a successful login: grep "Accepted password" /var/log/auth.log | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort -u
Cross-reference: any IP in both lists is a failures-then-success compromise candidate — escalate it per your IR plan.
Write offending IPs (more than 10 failures) to a blocklist file with timestamps for the firewall team.

checks.hint: Filter the failures: grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log
Extract the source IP field with awk '{print $(NF-3)}'

terminalMissions.title: Verify the download
terminalMissions.brief: A firmware file firmware.bin just landed in your lab directory. The vendor published SHA-256 9f86d081884c7d659a2feaa0c55ad015a3bf4f1b2b0b822cd15d6c15b0f00a08. Prove the file is intact before anyone installs it.
objectives: Compare it against the published value

checks.hint: In the Terminal tab, run `sha256sum firmware.bin`. The output digest must match the published value exactly.

terminalMissions.success_message: Hash matches — integrity verified. Install with confidence.

terminalMissions.title: Find the brute force
terminalMissions.brief: The SSH bastion feels sluggish. Pull the failed-password lines from the auth log and confirm whether an attack is underway.

checks.hint: In the Terminal tab, run `grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log`. Read the source IPs and usernames in the output.

terminalMissions.success_message: Evidence gathered — thousands of failures from a handful of IPs is a brute force, not typos. Block and harden.

terminalMissions.title: Authorized recon reasoning
terminalMissions.brief: You are authorized to assess the isolated lab subnet 10.20.30.0/24. Run a version scan and identify which hosts expose SSH — the same recon step an attacker would take, done here with written permission on a lab network.
objectives: Run a service version scan against the lab subnet

checks.hint: In the Terminal tab, run `nmap -sV 10.20.30.0/24`. Look for lines showing port 22/tcp as open. Only ever scan networks you own or are authorized to test.

terminalMissions.success_message: Recon complete — you now see the network the way an attacker maps it. Close what should not be open.

terminalMissions.title: Check the certificate expiry
terminalMissions.brief: Users report browser warnings on the intranet portal. A copy of its certificate, intranet.crt, is in your lab directory. Check whether expiry is the cause.

checks.hint: In the Terminal tab, run `openssl x509 -in intranet.crt -noout -dates`. Compare notAfter against today's date.

terminalMissions.success_message: Expiry confirmed or ruled out — either way, you read the certificate instead of guessing.

terminalMissions.title: Audit password aging
terminalMissions.brief: Policy says passwords expire every 90 days. Verify what the system actually enforces by reading the login defaults.

checks.hint: In the Terminal tab, run `grep -E "PASS_MAX_DAYS|PASS_MIN_LEN" /etc/login.defs`. Read the values, not just the names.

terminalMissions.success_message: Policy vs reality, compared. Report the gap or confirm compliance.

simulations.title: The midnight login storm
simulations.brief: It is 3:07 AM and the SIEM is paging: a burst of failed VPN logins from a dozen countries, then one success from a brand-new device. You are the analyst on call. Work it like the real thing.

steps.symptom: SIEM alert: 400 failed VPN logins in 20 minutes from 12 countries, then one successful login from an unrecognized device.
evidence:
02:47–03:07: 400 failed VPN logins, 12 source countries
03:08: SUCCESS — user m.reyes, new device fingerprint
Correlation: IMPOSSIBLE-TRAVEL + SPRAY-PATTERN
options: Ignore it — the success means the user finally remembered the password
Delete the SIEM rule to stop the paging
Isolate the account: disable VPN access and force a password plus MFA reset before investigating further
Email the user asking if it was them, and wait for a reply
steps.explain: A success immediately after distributed failures is a likely account takeover. Contain first — cut the account's access — then investigate. Waiting for an email reply gives the attacker hours.

steps.symptom: The user's laptop shows a remote-access tool installed yesterday and an active session to an unknown IP address.
evidence:
new process: remote-support-tool.exe (installed 22:14)
active session → 185.220.x.x (unknown)
user m.reyes: laptop lid closed since 21:30
options: Uninstall the tool and hand the laptop back — fastest recovery
Take a memory capture and disk image before remediation, then rebuild the host
Let the session run to see what the attacker does
Clear the SIEM logs to save disk space
steps.explain: Order of volatility: capture RAM and disk before you touch anything, because remediation destroys evidence. Then rebuild rather than clean — a compromised host cannot be trusted after in-place removal.

steps.symptom: Leadership asks what changes so this does not repeat next quarter.
evidence: VPN had no MFA. No impossible-travel alerting. IR plan last tested 18 months ago.
options: Require longer passwords only
Name and blame the user in the incident report
Change nothing — the attacker is gone
Enforce MFA on all VPN access, add impossible-travel alerting, and run a post-incident review with documented actions
steps.explain: The lessons-learned phase turns the incident into durable controls: MFA removes the single-factor failure, detection rules catch the next attempt earlier, and documented actions keep the fixes from evaporating.

simulations.debrief: You worked the full incident response lifecycle: detected via correlation, contained the account, preserved evidence before eradicating, and closed with lessons learned. That discipline is what the Security Operations domain rewards.

simulations.title: The invoice that was not
simulations.brief: Accounts payable forwards you an urgent wire instruction that supposedly came from the CFO. The CFO is unreachable on a flight. Walk the fraud attempt down step by step.

steps.symptom: Email to AP: urgent $85,000 wire for an acquisition, reply-to on a lookalike domain, marked strictly confidential.
evidence:
From: "CFO" <cfo@acrne-corp.com>
Reply-To: cfo@acrne-corp.com
Subject: STRICTLY CONFIDENTIAL — wire before market open
Body: do not call me, in meetings all day
options: Process the wire — the CFO's name is on it and it is marked confidential
Treat it as suspected BEC: do not reply, and verify out-of-band with the CFO on a known number
Reply asking for the CFO's mother's maiden name as verification
Forward it to the whole company as a warning, including the malicious links
steps.explain: The red flags are classic BEC: lookalike domain, urgency, secrecy, and do-not-call instructions. The defense is procedural — verify through a separate trusted channel before money moves. Never forward live lures to the whole company.

steps.symptom: The CFO's assistant confirms the CFO never sent the email. The message is fraudulent.
evidence:
Assistant (known number): CFO is airborne, sent no wire instructions.
Finance: no acquisition in progress.
options: Delete the email — problem solved
Reply to the attacker to waste their time
Report to security, preserve the full email with headers, and alert finance staff that this lure is active
Wire a $1 test payment to see what happens
steps.explain: Preserve the evidence (headers show the true origin), report through proper channels, and warn the targeted team — the same lure is likely hitting other inboxes. Deleting it destroys the trail.

steps.symptom: A second employee admits they wired $15,000 to a similar email last week and said nothing out of embarrassment.
evidence:
Last Tuesday: $15,000 wired to attacker-controlled account.
Funds likely moved through two intermediary banks.
options: Keep it quiet to avoid embarrassing the employee
Wait to see if the money comes back on its own
Fire the employee and close the case
Engage incident response and legal immediately and attempt a bank recall — time is critical
steps.explain: Fraud response is a race: bank recalls and law enforcement engagement lose value by the hour. Blame culture is what kept it hidden for a week — the fix is a no-blame reporting culture plus the callback verification process.

simulations.debrief: You spotted the BEC, verified out-of-band, preserved evidence, and escalated the real loss fast. Social engineering is defeated by process — and you just built the process.

simulations.title: The certificate that cried wolf
simulations.brief: The help desk queue is flooding: every browser shows a red warning on the internal HR portal. The certificate expired overnight. Fix it properly — and make sure it never happens again.

steps.symptom: NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID on the HR portal for all users. The certificate expired at midnight; the private key is intact on the server.
evidence:
notAfter=Oct 5 23:59:59 2026 GMT
today=Oct 6 08:12:00 2026 GMT
issuer: Internal CA (trusted)
options: Tell all users to click through the warning until next week
Confirm the scope (which services use this certificate), then reissue from the CA and deploy — communicate status only through official channels
Disable HTTPS on the portal so the warning goes away
Reboot the server; certificates fix themselves on restart
steps.explain: Scope first — the same cert may serve other hosts. Then reissue and deploy; expiry is routine operations, not an emergency redesign. Click-through trains users to ignore the warnings that catch real attacks.

steps.symptom: During renewal, a contractor suggests emailing the private key to the CA team to speed things up.
evidence: contractor: just send me the .key file and I'll get it signed in an hour
options: Send it — the CA team is trustworthy
Post it in the team chat so everyone can help
Refuse — generate the CSR locally; the private key never leaves the server
Encrypt it with a weak password and email it
steps.explain: The private key is the identity. Anyone who holds it can impersonate the server — no CA involvement needed. CSRs exist precisely so the key never travels: you send the signing request, keep the key.

steps.symptom: Leadership wants assurance this will not recur on the customer-facing storefront certificate.
evidence: 47 certificates across the estate; no central tracking; 3 expire within 60 days.
options: Buy 10-year certificates so nobody has to think about it
Assign an intern to check dates manually each morning
Nothing — expiry is rare and harmless
Deploy certificate expiry monitoring with 30/14/7-day alerts and automate renewal where possible
steps.explain: Undocumented certificates are future outages. Monitoring with escalating alerts plus automated renewal (ACME-style where supported) turns expiry from a crisis into a non-event. Long-lived certs just delay the same failure.

simulations.debrief: You scoped the outage, protected the private key, and built the monitoring that prevents the next one. That is PKI operations done right.

consoleSims.title: Harden the new web server
consoleSims.brief: The new web server goes live at noon. Policy is deny-by-default: open exactly one hole — HTTPS (TCP 443) from the corporate network 10.0.0.0/8 — then set the INPUT chain to DROP everything else.

tasks.instruction: Add an ACCEPT rule: INPUT, TCP 443, source 10.0.0.0/8.
tasks.hint: Rules tab → Add rule: CHAIN=INPUT, PROTOCOL=tcp, PORT=443, SOURCE=10.0.0.0/8, ACTION=ACCEPT

tasks.instruction: Set the INPUT chain default policy to DROP.

consoleSims.debrief: Order matters: the explicit allow must exist before the default deny, or you lock yourself out of the very service you're publishing. Least privilege, expressed in firewall rules.

consoleSims.title: Contain the crypto-miner
consoleSims.brief: The SIEM fired ALT-102: a malware hash match on a download — severity critical, host wkst-117. Work it like an analyst: acknowledge the alert, assign it to soc-tier1, then isolate the host.

tasks.hint: Alerts tab → click Ack on the ALT-102 row.
Assign alert form: ALERT ID=ALT-102, ANALYST=soc-tier1
Click 'Isolate host' on the ALT-102 row.

consoleSims.debrief: Acknowledge, assign, contain — the first three moves of incident-response triage. Isolation stops lateral movement while you investigate; it never deletes evidence.

consoleSims.title: Block the RDP brute-forcer
consoleSims.brief: Logs show 203.0.113.45 hammering RDP (TCP 3389). Drop that source on port 3389 — but keep RDP reachable for admins on the corporate network 10.0.0.0/8.

tasks.hint: Same form with SOURCE=10.0.0.0/8, ACTION=ACCEPT — management stays reachable.

consoleSims.debrief: Block the attacker, keep the admins: host-based firewall rules can be surgical. (And the long-term fix is never exposing RDP to the internet at all — VPN or jump host.)

consoleSims.title: Write the failed-login detector
consoleSims.brief: After last night's VPN login storm, build a detection rule that fires when one source IP racks up more than 20 failed logins — then escalate the open impossible-travel alert ALT-101 to incident response.

tasks.instruction: Create a detection rule named exactly: VPN failed-login burst — query: event:authfail | stats count by src_ip | where count > 20

params.name: VPN failed-login burst
params.query: event:authfail | stats count by src_ip | where count > 20

tasks.hint: Detection rules tab → Create rule: NAME=VPN failed-login burst, QUERY=event:authfail | stats count by src_ip | where count > 20
Alerts tab → click Escalate on the ALT-101 row.

consoleSims.debrief: Detection engineering is proactive defense: you turned one incident into a rule that catches the next one. Escalation hands the active threat to the incident-response process with full context.
